draft_sections.section: Contents (draft table of contents, 25 headings)
draft_sections.where: Contents page; whole book (9 parts, 27 chapters)
draft_sections.details: The draft's 25 headings were regrouped into 9 parts and 27 chapters ordered from easy to hard. Draft headings kept as chapters: Arabic vs English (Ch 4), Equivalence (Ch 10), Form vs meaning (Ch 5), Types of meaning and Sentence vs speaker meaning (merged into Ch 6), Collocation (Ch 8), Context and Homonymy vs polysemy (merged into Ch 7), Idioms (Ch 9), Literal and Free translation (merged into Ch 11), Metaphoric translation (Ch 12), the two 'Translation strategies' headings (merged into Ch 14, part of the second moved to Ch 17), Cultural approximation (Ch 15), Descriptive translation (Ch 16), Lexical creation (Ch 17), Analysing a text (Ch 18), Commentary (Ch 25), Terminology (Ch 21), AI and MT (Ch 22). New chapters were added for the notes' requests (Ch 2, 13, 19, 20, 3, 23, 24) and for the audiovisual notes (Ch 26, 27).
draft_sections.reason: The notes ask for a final structure and table of contents (para. 58) and for repeated material to be merged (paras 1, 8, 17); Report s. 6.1 gives the reason for each part's place.

draft_sections.details: Opening 'Language Structure Note'.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – 'we start with the verb' / English SVO, Arabic VSO
draft_sections.details: Rule softened: English usually SVO; formal Arabic often starts with the verb, but a subject-first (nominal) sentence is also correct. The term 'verbal sentence' was added.
draft_sections.reason: First review r1 #23 (high): 'Arabic usually starts with the verb' is a false generalisation – nominal sentences are grammatical and common in MSA.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – table example 'Sam ate the cake' (☒ سام اكل التفاحة / ☑ اكل سام التفاحة)
draft_sections.details: Arabic corrected to match the English ('cake', not 'apple': أكلَ سامٌ الكعكةَ); the subject-first version is no longer marked ✗ but labelled 'correct, but less usual'. A second example (the government announced new measures) was added.
draft_sections.reason: First review r1 #24 (high): marking a grammatical nominal sentence ✗ teaches that correct Arabic is wrong; the draft's Arabic also said 'apple' for 'cake'.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – 'He is in bed → نائم (not في السرير)'
draft_sections.details: Now إنه في فراشه or, depending on context, إنه نائم, rather than إنه في السرير.
draft_sections.reason: First review r1 #30–31: 'in bed' does not always mean asleep; في فراشه is the natural idiom.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – 'As an officer / As a Manager of the Company → بصفتي'
draft_sections.details: Same idea; Arabic corrected to بصفتي ضابطاً… (case ending) and بصفتي مديرَ الشركة…; 'I' added to the English so the first person matches; note that 'as' means a role, not كـ.
draft_sections.reason: First review r1 #33: بصفتي is first person but the English had no 'I'.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – note on nouns without a feminine (قاضي، نائب، ضابط)
draft_sections.details: Kept for قاضية and نائبة with the reason (other meanings 'fatal', 'calamity'), and updated: these titles are widely used today for women judges and MPs. ضابط dropped.
draft_sections.reason: Report s. 8.1: updated rather than removed so that the handbook reflects current usage.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – 'Shops stay open → تظل أو تبقى محلات تجارية'
draft_sections.details: Arabic completed and made a full sentence: تظلّ المحلات التجارية مفتوحة; the trap is explained ('stay' means 'remain', not 'live').
draft_sections.reason: First review r1 #34: the example did not say what the trap is.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – 'Eventually → في نهاية المطاف'
draft_sections.details: Same equivalent; explanation added ('in the end', not 'possibly').

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – 'is → تعد' and note 'تعد الترجمة تخصصاً… مثيراً للاهتمام'
draft_sections.details: Rule corrected: in the present tense Arabic normally leaves out 'is' (الترجمةُ مجالٌ شائق); تُعدّ is only an option in formal writing when the sentence gives an opinion. Added: do not translate a simple 'is' with يكون; use كان in the past; do and have.
draft_sections.reason: First review r1 #27 (high): presenting تُعدّ as the equivalent of 'is' adds meaning and encourages translationese; final review f1 #9–11 limited the يكون ban to a simple 'is'.

draft_sections.section: Arabic vs English – 'to see the Roman ruins → لمشاهدة / لزيارة / لرؤية'

draft_sections.reason: Three alternatives reduced to the most natural one, with the reason stated.
